name: Density HIFU

card.summary: Jeisys Medical's Density, a Korean non-invasive energy device (described by the maker as dual-mode radiofrequency, and often discussed alongside HIFU lifters) used in clinics to tighten skin on the face and body.
card.note: The maker describes Density as radiofrequency rather than ultrasound; efficacy figures are manufacturer-reported.

quick.overview:
Density is a skin-tightening device from the Korean company Jeisys Medical. It is frequently grouped with Korean HIFU lifting devices in online discussion, but the manufacturer describes it as a radiofrequency platform that sequentially delivers monopolar and bipolar RF energy with surface cooling.

The appearance goal is firmer skin, smoother texture and fewer fine lines on the face and body, with no needles and no downtime according to the maker. Supporting claims come from the manufacturer, and independent trial data were not found.
quick.how: A clinician moves a handpiece with a contact tip over the area while energy shots are delivered and the skin surface is cooled. Courses are typically repeated, and the maker says it can be used on face and body.
quick.risks: As with other energy-based skin devices, temporary redness or warmth may occur, and treatment is by a licensed practitioner. The maker states Density is approved by the US FDA and Korea MFDS without listing the cleared indications on its product page.

lead: Density is a skin-tightening platform from the South Korean company Jeisys Medical, used in clinics to firm and smooth the face and body without needles or incisions. Its maker describes it as a high-frequency radiofrequency (RF) device that applies monopolar RF, which is aimed at deeper dermal tissue, and bipolar RF, aimed at thinner, more superficial layers, in a single sequential pass [1]. Many patients and clinics file it with Korean 'HIFU' lifting machines because it is sold for the same purpose, and the Density name appears in lists of Jeisys devices that include true ultrasound lifters; technically, though, Density heats tissue with RF rather than focused ultrasound [1][2].

People use it for early to moderate skin laxity, crepey texture, fine lines and loss of firmness, with the aim of a tighter jawline and cheek contour and smoother-looking skin. One treating clinic describes it as suited to laxity and collagen loss from ageing or weight loss and also markets it as 'collagen banking', a proactive approach for younger patients [3].

The published human literature on Density itself is small: a five-patient case series from 2025, in which one author is a consultant to the manufacturer [4]. Related work includes a 2022 animal study of combined monopolar and bipolar RF in aged mouse skin [5] and a retrospective review of a different Jeisys device, an HIFU plus monopolar RF combination, in 56 patients [6].

chain: Collagen remodelling and tightening over time
angle.text: Clinics use Density to tighten skin on the face and body without surgery or downtime. The maker says results are immediate and long-lasting; these are manufacturer claims.

paras: The Density system consists of a console and a handpiece fitted with interchangeable contact tips. According to the manufacturer, the tips come in sizes for the eye area, the face, the body and a general-purpose 'Alpha' tip, each with a stated number of shots and treatment area; the face tip, for example, covers about 2 x 2 cm per shot and the body tip about 5 x 3.2 cm [1]. The console is listed as operating at 6.78 MHz with up to 400 W of output, with an automatic pulsing mode that removes the need to press a pedal for each pulse and a repetition rate of 1 to 3 Hz [1].

A cryogen gas-spray cooling system with five levels and real-time skin-temperature monitoring is intended to protect the surface and reduce discomfort, adjusting after each shot [1]. A feature called Realtime Impedance Calibration adjusts RF delivery to the electrical resistance of the tissue being treated [1]. A later version is sold under the name Density Noir [1].

Radiofrequency devices pass alternating current through the skin; resistance to that current produces heat in the dermis. In the monopolar mode, current travels from the tip through the body to a return pad, which tends to heat deeper; in the bipolar mode, current flows between nearby electrodes, which keeps heating shallower. Jeisys describes Density as delivering both in sequence under a patented heating algorithm (a Korean patent number is cited on its page) so that deep and superficial layers are warmed in one treatment [1]. A clinic's explanation likewise says the monopolar component is aimed at long-term collagen remodelling and the bipolar component at immediate surface tightening [3].

The stated rationale is that controlled heating contracts existing collagen and stimulates fibroblasts to make new collagen and elastin over following weeks, producing firmer skin [3]. The manufacturer reports histology showing more newly synthesised collagen, and clinics repeat figures of a 239 percent increase in newly synthesised collagen, 76 percent in collagen fibre density and 82 percent in elastin fibre density; these figures are manufacturer-reported and the clinic page notes results vary by patient [1][3].

High-intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU) aims multiple ultrasound beams at a small focal point, where tissue can reach roughly 65 to 85 degrees C [2]. Cosmetic HIFU machines use this principle at depth in the skin and underlying tissue layers. Density's own materials describe RF heating only and do not mention ultrasound [1]. The 'HIFU' in the entry's common name therefore reflects how it is grouped in online discussion rather than its mechanism.

Treatment is performed by a clinician who moves the tip over the face or body in a grid of shots while the cooling system works. In the 2025 case series, a session took about 40 minutes, used 10 to 12 passes with continuous contact cooling and no anaesthesia, and was followed for three months [4]. A clinic describes topical numbing being applied beforehand and calls the procedure needle-free and 'without any downtime' [3]. The manufacturer says the right number of shots depends on skin condition and treatment area [1].

Clinics describe it as one of several Korean energy-based options for skin tightening, alongside ultrasound-based lifters and other RF devices, and patients commonly look at before-and-after photographs on clinic and company pages. The manufacturer's page shows photographs at four weeks without quantitative measurements [1].

Jeisys states that Density is approved by the US FDA and certified by Korea's MFDS; its page does not list the clearance details or indications, and it gives no adverse-event data [1]. In the 2025 case series, no adverse events were reported: there were no pigmentary changes, burns or scarring, and patients rated discomfort at 2 to 3 out of 10 [4]. In the related Jeisys HIFU plus RF review, all 56 patients had transient mild erythema and no serious adverse events were recorded [6]. As with other thermal skin devices, treatment is carried out by licensed practitioners; the manufacturer advises consulting a medical expert [1].

Lin and Kumar published a descriptive case series in Clinical, Cosmetic and Investigational Dermatology in November 2025 on five adults aged 40 to 61 (four women, one man) of Fitzpatrick skin type IV with photoaging and laxity. Each received one session with the High F-tip and was assessed at one and three months. The authors reported improvements in firmness, texture and facial contour, most visible in the lower and lateral face, reduced wrinkle area and pore visibility, aesthetic scores of 3 to 5 out of 5 and a visible brow lift in three patients [4].

The authors state that the series had no control group, no blinding, no objective imaging or histology, no statistical analysis and only a three-month follow-up, and describe the findings as preliminary; one author discloses a consulting role with Jeisys [4].

A 2022 animal study (Oh, Rho and colleagues, International Journal of Molecular Sciences) compared monopolar-then-bipolar and bipolar-then-monopolar RF sequences in aged mouse skin and reported increased expression of NRF2, GLO-1 and M2 macrophage markers after RF, interpreted as lowering accumulation of advanced glycation end-products and raising skin elasticity [5]. The manufacturer cites this paper on the Density product page [1].

A retrospective study in Malaysia (Khong and colleagues, 2024) examined 56 patients treated with a Jeisys HIFU device (Q+) combined with a monopolar RF device (ACGEN), not Density. Three researchers scored photographs; 54 of 56 patients (96.4 percent) were rated improved on the Global Aesthetic Improvement Scale. The authors noted the small sample, no randomised control and photographs taken only immediately after treatment [6].

timeline.event: Oh, Rho and colleagues publish an aged-mouse study comparing combined monopolar and bipolar RF sequences, later cited by Jeisys on the Density page [5][1].
Khong and colleagues publish a retrospective review of a Jeisys HIFU plus monopolar RF combination in 56 Malaysian patients [6].
Lin and Kumar publish a five-patient case series of Density RF for facial photoaging and laxity [4].
